RTAI: Closed-end funds that hold municipal bonds, bought when they trade at discounts to the value of their bonds, paying tax-advantaged income. The closed-end structure adds a second layer of movement, since discounts can widen or narrow on top of bond prices.
CBOJ: A structured outcome fund on bitcoin over a one-year period ending each January, joining bitcoin's gains up to a cap while adding protection against declines beyond a set point. It is bitcoin exposure with the edges trimmed, for investors wary of the full plunge.
TIME: Large US growth companies, mostly technology, combined with a hedge position that bets against the Nasdaq-100. Carrying a built-in hedge is unusual for a core equity fund: it trims losses in tech-led sell-offs but drags when tech rallies.
XTOC: Options on the S&P 500 aiming for accelerated gains up to a preset cap over a one-year period starting each October. It is a leveraged-style bet on a rising market, carrying full losses when the index falls.
FARX: A conservative global mix of short-term bonds, trend-following futures funds, commodities and floating-rate Treasuries, run for absolute returns rather than against a benchmark. It aims to make modest progress in most markets, accepting that it will trail in strong bull runs.
ITDJ: A target date portfolio for retirement around 2070, currently invested almost entirely in stock funds covering US large, small and international companies. The mix will glide toward bonds as 2070 approaches, so today it is built for maximum long-term growth.
DVGR: US companies with a rare record: raising their dividends by double digits on average for at least ten straight years without a single cut. That strict screen favors proven growers across technology, health care and finance, and it rules out most dividend payers.
TEKX: Companies accelerating transformative technology: crypto miners, data center builders, energy innovators and chip firms. It mixes the crypto economy with the AI buildout, so it is volatile and heavily influenced by bitcoin's mood.
ACSM: Small and mid-sized US companies chosen by Hartford's alpha capture process, which gathers ideas from across its investment teams into one portfolio. It aims to beat the Russell 2500 group of smaller companies through breadth of ideas rather than a few big bets.
MRGR: A merger arbitrage portfolio: shares of companies being acquired, bought after deals are announced in hopes of capturing the gap to the takeover price. It aims for steady, deal-driven gains mostly independent of the market, with the risk that a deal collapses.
JLQD: Mostly investment grade corporate bonds in US dollars, with some mortgage-backed securities mixed in, actively managed with sustainability criteria. It aims for core bond income while screening out issuers the managers judge weak on environmental and social grounds.
DANA: High-quality bonds chosen to preserve capital: agency mortgage bonds, US government securities and corporate bonds rated AA or better. It aims for steady income with limited volatility, accepting modest yields as the price of safety.
RCLR: Middle slices of collateralized loan obligations rated from BBB down to B, with income reinvested rather than paid out. Reinvestment compounds the higher yields of these riskier CLO layers, and losses can mount if the underlying company loans sour.
SHRY: Large and mid-sized US companies that return the most cash to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks combined. That shareholder yield focus tilts it toward mature, cash-generating firms in finance, media and technology rather than fast growers.
IBMV: Municipal bonds that mature during 2033, paying interest exempt from federal income tax, in a fund set to close at the end of 2033. Like other term muni funds, it returns principal as bonds mature, suiting money with a known future use.
OCTH: Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 that pay income unless the index falls past a barrier set 20 percent below its starting level. If the barrier breaks, the income stops cushioning and the fund shares the market's decline.
IQGR: Quality growth companies outside the US, picked actively across finance, technology and industry in developed and emerging markets. It looks for durable growers abroad, and currency movements add their own layer to the returns.
SMRF: Nuclear energy companies: uranium miners, reactor builders and firms developing small modular reactors, plus the technology around them. It is a bet on nuclear power's comeback as grids hunt for clean, always-on electricity for data centers and industry.
ZTOP: High yield bonds from the 100 largest junk bond issuers, the biggest borrowers in the below-investment-grade market. Sticking to the largest issuers keeps it in more liquid bonds, though the credit risk of junk debt remains.
PZIV: Non-US companies trading at deep discounts to what the managers believe they are truly worth, spread across finance, industry, health care and consumer shares. Pzena's patient value style can look out of step for years before bargains pay off.
FTHB: Bonds from issuers screened as biblically aligned, led by US Treasuries, with corporate bonds, mortgage bonds and preferred shares behind. It targets income for faith-based investors, and the values screen rules out some big borrowers entirely.
MEME: Meme stocks: companies caught up in social media frenzies, with heavy trading and extreme price swings driven by online attention. Holdings rotate toward whatever is trending, making this a speculation tool rather than an investment in the usual sense.
SDUR: Short-term investment grade debt: corporate bonds, asset-backed and mortgage securities and government bonds with brief maturities. It aims for income a step above cash with low volatility, suiting money that cannot afford big price swings.
KHYB: US dollar bonds from Asia-Pacific borrowers, including banks and companies in frontier markets like Mongolia, paying high income for the region. Dollar denomination removes local currency risk, but the borrowers include weaker credits far from the region's giants.
BOXA: US aggregate bond exposure built entirely from options contracts rather than by owning bonds, using option spreads engineered to mimic a broad bond index. The options-based design is unusual and can cut some of the costs and risks of holding thousands of bonds.
BHDG: A bitcoin tail-risk strategy: protective put options on bitcoin funds, paid for by selling call options, with most assets in bonds and cash. It is built to cushion a crypto crash, and in calm or rising markets the insurance cost drags on returns.
NXTI: US companies rich in intangible capital: research, brands, software and know-how that outweigh their physical assets relative to book value. That lens favors modern, asset-light businesses across technology, retail and health care over factories and heavy industry.
TYLG: Technology stocks from the S&P 500 with call options sold on only part of the position, leaving more room to grow than a full covered call fund. It splits the difference between income and growth in the tech sector.
DDTA: Options on the S&P 500 designed to gain from modest moves in either direction over a one-year period starting each April, with a 10 percent buffer against drops. It is built for choppy, sideways markets, and big one-way moves can leave it behind.
DLAG: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to gain when the market moves up or down by a moderate amount over a one-year period ending each August. It is built for sideways or mildly trending markets, while a sharp move in one direction can leave it behind.
UUPP: Collateralized loan obligations, bundles of loans to companies, bought across their different risk layers rather than only the safest top slice. Reaching down the layers raises the income, and the managers choose how much risk to take as credit conditions change.
NBGX: Large US growth companies picked through research that mixes number crunching with judgment, led by the biggest technology names. It is a concentrated growth portfolio, so it lives and dies by a few dozen large stocks.
FPRO: Real estate companies and trusts: warehouse landlords, data centers, cell towers, shopping centers and apartment owners, mostly in the US. It pays property income through a semi-transparent active fund, so the full holdings list is not published every day.
QBF: Bitcoin exposure with a floor under losses over each three-month period, while leaving gains uncapped above that floor. The floor is set 20 percent down, so deep quarterly crashes are trimmed while ordinary dips are still felt in full.
CPNM: Options on the Nasdaq-100 structured to protect against losses over a one-year period ending in March, while taking part in gains up to a cap. It trades away the biggest rallies in exchange for a much softer landing when tech stocks fall.
XLII: Industrial companies from the S&P 500: airlines, defense contractors, machinery, railroads and logistics firms, paired with an options overlay that collects premium income. The options add regular payouts on top of a cyclical sector, in exchange for part of the upside.
BOUT: Stocks picked as they break out above their recent trading ranges, using Investor's Business Daily methods to spot the start of sustained runs. The current mix leans into health care, and breakout strategies can suffer strings of false starts in choppy markets.
OCTJ: Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 that pay income unless the index falls past a barrier set 30 percent below its starting level. The deeper barrier keeps income flowing through moderate sell-offs, but a crash still passes losses through.
CRSH: An options strategy that profits when Tesla's stock falls, using inverse exposure to the electric car maker plus income from sold options. It is a bearish single-stock tool: it gains in Tesla drops, loses when Tesla climbs, and pays income along the way.
PBOT: Artificial intelligence and automation companies worldwide: chip designers, equipment makers, software platforms and cybersecurity firms. Technology makes up about nine tenths of the fund, so it is a broad AI wager rather than a bet on one kind of AI business.
FECM: Intermediate-term municipal bonds from across the US, paying interest exempt from federal income tax, actively managed by First Eagle. It targets steady tax-free income with moderate swings, the middle ground of the muni market.
TESL: A concentrated Tesla strategy: a large direct stake in Tesla's stock amplified with call options, while the rest sits in Treasury bills. It magnifies life as a Tesla shareholder, bigger gains in rallies and deeper pain in drops, all on one company.
ARWG: US growth companies of many sizes, led by technology, with industry, health care and consumer names behind, including special situations the managers expect to be revalued. It is a broad growth hunt that depends on stock picking more than sector calls.
PCFI: Floating rate loans and securities, mostly bank loans made to companies, whose interest payments reset as market rates change. When rates rise its income rises too, making it a rare bond fund that can welcome higher rates, though the borrowers are often leveraged firms.
MPIA: Exposure through swaps to an autocall index built on the Nasdaq-100 with an accelerator feature that can boost coupon payoffs. It aims for enhanced income tied to big tech, with early redemption possible and losses if the index falls far enough.
WTRE: Real estate built for the new economy: data centers, cell towers, logistics warehouses and the landlords behind them, worldwide. It ties property income to digital demand rather than shops and offices, though it still moves with interest rates like other property funds.
HDMV: Developed-market companies outside the US chosen for low expected volatility, heavy in banks, utilities and property firms in places like Hong Kong, Singapore and Australia. It aims for a calmer international ride, often lagging when markets surge.
QRMI: The Nasdaq-100's technology-led stocks wrapped in a collar: put options bought for protection and call options sold to pay for them and add income. The collar trims both the worst drops and the best rallies, suiting investors who fear big tech's swings.
PSCU: Small US companies in two steadier industries, utilities and communication services, from rural power and water firms to satellite and media names. Small size makes these normally calm industries livelier than usual, an unusual mix of caution and spice.
BULD: Companies engineering the future: robotics, 3D printing, design software and the chip equipment behind them, from around the world. Technology is about four fifths of the fund, making it a growth bet on how things get designed and made.
